analysis.one_liner: Ends tax deductions for tobacco companies' legal settlement payments and sends the savings to medical research.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan bill with 15 Senate cosponsors never got a hearing or vote in the Senate Finance Committee and died when the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.
analysis.plain_summary: In 1997, tobacco companies were negotiating a huge national settlement with state and federal governments. Under existing tax rules, those settlement payments would have counted as a normal business expense, meaning the companies could subtract them from their taxable income and federal taxpayers would effectively foot part of the bill. This bill would have barred that deduction and directed the extra tax revenue into a new National Institutes of Health trust fund for health research.
analysis.who_benefits: Federal taxpayers, who would no longer subsidize tobacco companies' settlement payments through the tax code, and medical research, which would receive the resulting revenue through a dedicated NIH trust fund covering AIDS research, minority health, women's health, and other programs.

how_it_helps.text: The bill adds a new section to the tax code stating that no deduction is allowed for any amount paid to federal, state, or local governments under a tobacco judgment or settlement, including the tobacco industry settlement agreement of June 20, 1997.

It creates an NIH Trust Fund for Health Research into which the net revenue gain from ending the deduction is automatically deposited, with distributions to NIH institutes including the Office of AIDS Research.
The bill requires tobacco companies to report on their tax returns the total settlement payments for which a deduction is disallowed, adding transparency.
The trust fund includes a trigger so its money is spent only if regular NIH appropriations do not shrink, meaning the new money adds to rather than replaces existing research funding.

analysis.who_pays: Tobacco companies, whose settlement payments would become a full after-tax cost instead of a partly tax-subsidized one. Depending on how it changed the companies' appetite for settling litigation, smokers could eventually face higher prices.

drawbacks.text: Ending the deduction raises the true net cost of settling to tobacco companies, which could have made them less willing to agree to a national settlement and prolonged litigation instead of producing compensation and public-health restrictions.

The trust fund is tied entirely to revenue from settlement payments, so if no large settlement or judgment occurred, the fund would receive little or nothing and the promised research money would not materialize.

Some would object that denying a business deduction treats tobacco litigation costs differently from other legal expenses, a departure from the normal rule that costs of doing business are deductible.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core change is simple and targeted: a company paying damages for harm from its product would no longer get a federal tax write-off for it, and the revenue would be earmarked for medical research with safeguards so it does not replace existing NIH funding. The main risk is that a heavier after-tax settlement bill could give the industry one more reason to walk away from the negotiating table, though the settlement at issue in 1997 ultimately collapsed for many other reasons anyway.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, markup, or vote; it died when the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999.

narrative.text: Sen. Connie Mack introduced the bill on November 7, 1997, with introductory remarks on the Senate floor.
Fifteen senators cosponsored the bill: 9 Democrats and 6 Republicans, giving it clear bipartisan support from the start.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance, where it stayed for the rest of the Congress.
No further action appears in the record: no hearing, no committee markup, no floor vote, and the Congress ended on January 3, 1999.

The bill was written against the backdrop of the tobacco industry settlement agreement of June 20, 1997, which it specifically referenced, and any payments under whatever legislation implemented that settlement would also have been non-deductible.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Tobacco companies kept the ability to deduct government settlement payments as a business expense, leaving federal taxpayers to absorb part of those costs through the tax code, and no dedicated NIH research fund was created.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Tobacco companies and their tax treatment

sides.party_line_note: The bill's 15 cosponsors split 9 Democrats and 6 Republicans, so its cosponsorship was bipartisan; its failure came from committee inaction rather than a floor vote split by party.

industries.note: The bill would have made every dollar paid to governments in tobacco judgments and settlements a full after-tax cost instead of a tax-deductible business expense, costing the industry tens of billions of dollars over the life of a national settlement. Because the bill died, the industry kept the deduction and the public kept subsidizing part of those payments through the tax code.

The bill would have automatically deposited the revenue gain into a dedicated NIH trust fund for health research, including AIDS, minority health, and women's health programs, creating a new funding stream for research grants and facilities. With the bill's death, that funding never materialized.
